How we calculate running costs

Appliances measured in watts: cost = power (kW) × hours used × share of time at full power × your unit rate. Thermostatic appliances such as ovens and heaters switch on and off, so each page states the share it assumes.

Appliances that run in cycles (washing machines, dishwashers, tumble dryers): cost = kWh per cycle × your unit rate. Use the figure on your energy label for accuracy.

Always-on appliances (fridges and freezers): cost = kWh per year from the energy label × your unit rate.

Seasonal appliances: heaters, dehumidifiers and fans are counted only for the months they're typically used. You can change this on each page.

Unit rate: the default is the Ofgem price cap average for 1 Oct – 31 Dec 2026 (standard variable tariff, Direct Debit, England, Scotland & Wales).: 26.32p/kWh. Fixed, Economy 7, EV and other time-of-use tariffs, and regional rates, differ, so you can enter your own; we remember it on your device.

Standing charge: not included, because you pay it whether the appliance is used or not.

Typical figures: default wattages come from the Centre for Sustainable Energy's "What uses watt?" table where it lists the appliance, and from typical manufacturer ranges otherwise. Each page names its source.

Last updated 2026-11-16.

Costs use the Ofgem price cap average for 1 Oct – 31 Dec 2026 (standard variable tariff, Direct Debit, England, Scotland & Wales). Your rate may differ: tap the rate at the top of any page to use your own. Figures are estimates for typical appliances; check your appliance's label for its actual power.

Your electricity unit rate

This is the pence per kWh on your bill or app. Don't use the standing charge: you pay that whether an appliance is on or not. On Economy 7 or an EV tariff, use the rate for the time the appliance runs.
